claims.text: The 9 January 2018 DIA list credits item 26, "Aneutronic Fusion Propulsion", to "Dr V Teofilo, Lockheed Martin".

Teofilo held a PhD in physics from New York University, taught at Princeton where he operated the university nuclear reactor, worked on fusion reactor development at Westinghouse, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Physics International and Bechtel, and spent 28 years at Lockheed Martin Space Systems. He died 10 January 2026, aged 81.

label: Vincent L. Teofilo
narrative:
Vincent Louis Teofilo was a career industrial physicist whose path ran through almost every institution that has ever tried to build a fusion reactor in the United States. He took a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering at Manhattan College and a master's in nuclear engineering and a PhD in physics at New York University. He taught at Princeton and operated the university's nuclear reactor, then worked on fusion reactor development at Westinghouse, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Physics International and Bechtel. He then spent twenty-eight years at Lockheed Martin Space Systems, contributing to programmes including the Hubble Space Telescope and the Space-Based Infrared System. He died on 10 January 2026 at the age of 81.

That combination, deep fusion plasma physics plus long service inside a prime contractor's space division, is exactly the profile AAWSAP needed for a propulsion deliverable that had to be credible to a defence-warning audience rather than to a physics journal. Three of the 38 DIRDs went to Lockheed Martin staff, Teofilo on aneutronic fusion, S. Macheret on MHD air-breathing propulsion and J. Golightly on ultracapacitors, which makes Lockheed Martin the single most heavily represented corporate institution on the DIRD author list.

Teofilo's DIRD is not a physics monograph. It runs from confinement schemes through Hall thrusters to a roadmap figure, surveys the funding levels of privately backed fusion start-ups, and closes by arguing that the physicists who pioneered the reactor technology must now work alongside the space systems companies. It reads as an industrial technology-transition assessment, which is what a Lockheed Martin space-systems physicist would be expected to produce. He is also recorded as a co-author of "Review of Experimental Concepts for Studying the Quantum Vacuum Field", placing him adjacent to the EarthTech vacuum-energy literature.
